1969 Dodge Super Bee With Day-Two Sunroof Is a Sad One-of-None Field Find
11 photos
Photo: Auto Archaeology/YouTube
Introduced in 1968, the Super Bee was Dodge's entry-level muscle car. It was also largely similar to the Plymouth Road Runner. But while the latter became pretty popular, the Super Bee moved far fewer units. By the time it was discontinued in 1971, the Super Bee had sold about 56,000 units. For reference, Plymouth delivered over 170,000 Road Runners over the same period.
About half of these Super Bees were sold during the 1969 model year, when 27,800 customers left showrooms driving one. The Super Bee was available with three powerplants that year. The muscle car came standard with the 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, which was rated at 335 horsepower. The optional 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi, good for 425 horsepower, was still available.
The third powerplant was brand-new for 1969. I'm talking about the six-barrel version of the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB (also called the Six-Pack). Rated at 390 horsepower, it was part of the A12 package, which included heavy-duty components for drag racing.
The Hemi Super Bee saw daylight in only 166 units, while the Six-Pack engine found its way into 1,907 examples. The remaining 25,727 cars were ordered with the base 383-cubic-inch big-block V8. Some of these cars are still on the road today and pop up for sale at public auctions. Most of them, however, are still rotting away in junkyards and barns. The green example you see here is one of the unlucky ones.
Documented by Ryan Brutt of YouTube's "Auto Archaeology," this Mopar has been sitting in the same spot since the 1980s. And that spot is among the worst for a steel classic: a farm field. It usually comes with full exposure to the elements, moisture, and total neglect. Unfortunately, one owner also opted to sell many parts, so the Super Bee is a sad sight today.
Once a gorgeous F8 green muscle car, the Dodge is now covered in surface rust, and it's missing both the hood and the front grille assembly. The drivetrain was also removed, and the interior doesn't look better either. The latter still has some of its original features in place, but the floor panels are nearly gone. As a result, there's a tree growing through the cabin, and it has already extended beyond the roof.
Interestingly enough, this Super Bee also has a sunroof opening. As you may already know, golden-era muscle cars with sunroofs are quite rare . It was a brand-new option at the time, and sales were still low, often enough in two- or three-digit territory. But this Super Bee wasn't actually born with a sunroof.
1969 was the first year when Chrysler had the feature on the options list. However, it was only offered on the Charger that year. Only 391 units were ordered with one, including 131 R/T models. The sunroof option was extended to the Challenger in 1970 but didn't find its way onto the Super Bee until 1971. Only nine cars were ordered with it that year.
The cutout you see here is a day-two addition. It was probably added sometime in the mid-to-late-1970s, when sunroofs became popular, but the entire assembly is missing. Our host says that the car was drag-raced by a local guy, but there's no relevant info on that.
Is this Super Bee worth saving? Well, I'd say it still has a few usable components, including the door panels, the rear taillight panel, and maybe a few body elements. A restoration is a different story, though. This Mopar requires a six-figure investment at this point, and it's definitely not worth it relative to its market value. But it's still sad seeing it like this.
